items.title: Nobody called it the Wars of the Roses at the time
items.claim: The wars between Lancaster and York (1455-1487) are remembered for the red and white rose badges. What is the actual history of those symbols?

options.text: Both sides wore rose badges throughout the conflict
The white rose was a Yorkist badge, but the red Lancastrian rose was largely a Tudor-era invention — Henry VII used the union of the roses as propaganda
The roses came from heraldic tradition dating to the Conquest
The name was coined in 1485 by Henry VII himself

items.reveal_title: The Tudor rose was the spin
items.reveal:
Edward IV used a white rose among other badges. The red rose was a minor Lancastrian badge under Henry IV but rarely used during the wars themselves. The 'Tudor rose' (red and white combined) was created after Henry VII married Elizabeth of York in 1486 — the union as legitimising symbol.

The name 'Wars of the Roses' was popularised by Walter Scott's novel 'Anne of Geierstein' (1829). Shakespeare's 'Henry VI Part 1' invented the Temple Garden scene where nobles pluck the rival roses.
items.why: Historical memory is shaped by later spin. The Tudor regime had every reason to dramatise dynastic union; Shakespeare amplified the imagery; Scott named it. Almost none of that was visible in 1460.

items.title: The Great Fire of London killed officially six people
items.claim: The Great Fire (2-6 September 1666) destroyed much of the medieval City. Official deaths?

options.text: Six officially recorded — though modern historians suspect more, especially among the poor

items.reveal:
The fire destroyed 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches and St Paul's Cathedral over four days. It started at Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane around 1 a.m. on 2 September. Samuel Pepys's diary is the most vivid account.

Only six deaths were officially recorded. Neil Hanson and others have argued the true toll was higher — the fire reached temperatures over 1,700 C, hot enough to vaporise human remains, and many of the poor were not formally counted.

The Great Plague of 1665 had killed around 100,000 — perhaps a quarter of London's population — the previous year.
items.why: Official numbers are not the whole story, but they're also not nothing. The plague (100,000) and the fire (six) sit oddly together in memory, but both shaped Restoration London.

items.title: Joan of Arc was burned at Rouen in 1431, aged 19
items.claim: What did Joan of Arc achieve before her execution?

options.text: Nothing — her story is later legend

She convinced Charles VII she had divine guidance, led French forces to relieve the siege of Orléans in May 1429, helped recover Reims and have Charles crowned (July 1429); captured by Burgundians, sold to the English, tried for heresy and burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431
She was a Burgundian general who switched sides
She was canonised within months of her death

items.reveal:
Joan was a peasant from Domrémy who claimed visions of St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret from age 13. After persuading Charles's court at Chinon, she joined the relief of Orléans aged 17. The siege was lifted in nine days; Reims (the traditional coronation city) was retaken; Charles VII was crowned on 17 July 1429.

She was captured at Compiègne (May 1430), held for ransom by the Burgundians, sold to the English, and tried by a French ecclesiastical court at Rouen. The trial of 1455-56 (after the English left) annulled the conviction. She was canonised in 1920.

The Hundred Years War ended in French victory at Castillon (1453).
items.why: The Hundred Years War's turning point is a teenager with no military training. Joan of Arc's trial transcripts survive — she remains one of the most documented medieval figures and a case in how religion, war and gender intersect.
